(CNN) -- After weeks of controversy over Michael Mukasey's views on waterboarding, the Senate late Thursday approved the former judge's nomination for attorney general by a 53-40 vote. Waterboarding threatened to derail the approval of President Bush's nominee to lead the Justice Department. President Bush nominated Mukasey to replace longtime ally Alberto Gonzales, who resigned in September. The nomination had been considered at risk after a number of Democratic senators opposed Mukasey because of questions that arose from his views on the terror interrogation technique known as waterboarding and the president's power to order electronic surveillance. Mukasey, a former federal judge in New York, told senators he considers waterboarding "repugnant," but he could not categorically say whether the technique amounts to torture, which U.S. and international law bans. Waterboarding is a technique that involves restraining a suspect and pouring water on him to produce the sensation of drowning. Mukasey's confirmation was all but assured last week when two key Democrats on the Senate Judiciary Committee -- Sens. Dianne Feinstein of California and Chuck Schumer of New York -- said they would vote in favor of Mukasey despite the controversy. "The Department of Justice, once the crown jewel among government institutions, is adrift and rudderless," Schumer said Tuesday -- the same day the committee voted 11-8 to send Mukasey's nomination to the Senate floor. "It desperately needs a strong and independent leader at the helm to set it back on course and I believe Judge Mukasey is that person." Schumer said that in a meeting Friday the nominee said that Congress would be within its rights to pass a law that bans waterboarding across all government agencies and that the president "would have absolutely no legal authority to ignore" it. Schumer said he believed Mukasey would be more likely to find waterboarding illegal than an interim attorney general. "Indeed, his written answers to our notices have demonstrated more openness to ending the practices we abhor than either of this president's previous attorney general nominees have." But Mukasey's pledge to enforce such a law rang hollow with Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, the Judiciary Committee's chairman. "Some have sought to find comfort in Judge Mukasey's personal assurance that he would enforce a future, new law against waterboarding if this Congress were to pass one," Leahy said Tuesday. "Unsaid, of course, is the fact that any such prohibition would have to be enacted over the veto of this president." However, the committee's ranking Republican, Sen. Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania, said he believed Mukasey would enforce a law banning waterboarding. "He could have said a lot of things which would have given me more assurances," Specter said earlier. "But he is intelligent; he's really learned in the law. He's strong, ethical, honest beyond any question. He's not an intimate of the president." A majority of Americans consider waterboarding a form of torture, but some of those say it's OK for the U.S. government to use the technique, according to a poll released Tuesday. Asked whether they think waterboarding is a form of torture, more than two-thirds of respondents, or 69 percent, said yes; 29 percent said no. Asked whether they think the U.S. government should be allowed to use the procedure to try to get information from suspected terrorists, 58 percent said no; 40 percent said yes. The CNN/Opinion Research Corp. telephone poll of 1,024 American adults was carried out over the weekend and had a sampling error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. E-mail to a friend .

(CNN) -- After weeks of controversy over Michael Mukasey’s views on waterboarding, the Senate voted late Thursday to confirm the former judge as attorney general, approving his nomination by a 53-40 margin.

The issue of waterboarding had threatened to derail President Bush’s nominee to lead the Justice Department. Bush nominated Mukasey to replace longtime ally Alberto Gonzales, who resigned in September.

Mukasey’s nomination had been considered at risk after several Democratic senators opposed him over questions about his views on the terror interrogation technique known as waterboarding, as well as the president’s authority to order electronic surveillance.

Mukasey, a former federal judge in New York, told senators that he considered waterboarding “repugnant,” but said he could not state categorically whether the technique constitutes torture, which is prohibited under U.S. and international law. Waterboarding involves restraining a suspect and pouring water on him to create the sensation of drowning.

Mukasey’s confirmation was all but assured last week when two key Democrats on the Senate Judiciary Committee -- Sens. Dianne Feinstein of California and Chuck Schumer of New York -- said they would vote in favor of his nomination despite the controversy.

“The Department of Justice, once the crown jewel among government institutions, is adrift and rudderless,” Schumer said Tuesday, the same day the committee voted 11-8 to send Mukasey’s nomination to the Senate floor. “It desperately needs a strong and independent leader at the helm to set it back on course, and I believe Judge Mukasey is that person.”

Schumer said that, in a meeting Friday, Mukasey stated that Congress would be within its rights to pass a law banning waterboarding across all government agencies, and that the president “would have absolutely no legal authority to ignore” such a law.

Schumer also said he believed Mukasey would be more likely than an interim attorney general to determine that waterboarding is illegal. “Indeed, his written answers to our notices have demonstrated more openness to ending the practices we abhor than either of this president’s previous attorney general nominees have.”

But Mukasey’s pledge to enforce such a law rang hollow for Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, chairman of the Judiciary Committee.

“Some have sought to find comfort in Judge Mukasey’s personal assurance that he would enforce a future, new law against waterboarding if this Congress were to pass one,” Leahy said Tuesday. “Unsaid, of course, is the fact that any such prohibition would have to be enacted over the veto of this president.”

However, the committee’s ranking Republican, Sen. Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania, said he believed Mukasey would enforce a law banning waterboarding.

“He could have said a lot of things which would have given me more assurances,” Specter said earlier. “But he is intelligent; he’s really learned in the law. He’s strong, ethical, honest beyond any question. He’s not an intimate of the president.”

According to a poll released Tuesday, a majority of Americans consider waterboarding a form of torture, though some who hold that view also say the U.S. government should be permitted to use the technique.

Asked whether they consider waterboarding a form of torture, more than two-thirds of respondents -- 69 percent -- said yes, while 29 percent said no. Asked whether the U.S. government should be allowed to use the procedure to try to obtain information from suspected terrorists, 58 percent said no, while 40 percent said yes.

The CNN/Opinion Research Corp. telephone poll of 1,024 American adults was conducted over the weekend and had a sampling error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points.

WASHINGTON — The Senate confirmed Michael B. Mukasey as attorney general Thursday night by a vote of 53-40, ending a contentious nomination fight dominated by questions over the legality of waterboarding and the Bush administration’s interrogation policies.

Mukasey, a retired federal judge from New York, was nominated to replace Alberto Gonzales, who resigned after months of controversy over the firing of U.S. attorneys and allegations that the Justice Department had become politicized. Although Mukasey initially drew praise from senators in both parties for his judicial experience and independence, his confirmation became uncertain after he refused to say whether waterboarding — an interrogation technique that simulates drowning — is illegal torture.

During confirmation hearings, Mukasey called waterboarding “repugnant” and said torture is unconstitutional, but he declined to make a definitive legal judgment on the technique without access to classified information and internal Justice Department analysis. That position angered many Democrats and some human rights advocates, who argued that the United States has long regarded waterboarding as torture.

Sen. Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., who had recommended Mukasey to the White House, defended his decision to support the nomination despite expressing disappointment in Mukasey’s answers on interrogation. Schumer said Mukasey was not the nominee he would have chosen on every issue but argued that the Justice Department urgently needed new leadership and that Mukasey would be an improvement over the previous regime.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, D-Vt., opposed the nomination, saying Mukasey’s refusal to clearly condemn waterboarding raised serious doubts about whether he would restore the rule of law at the department. Leahy said the attorney general must be able to tell the president no when government conduct violates the law.

Sen. Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania, the Judiciary Committee’s ranking Republican, supported Mukasey, saying the nominee had demonstrated integrity and independence. Specter said Mukasey’s confirmation was necessary to stabilize the Justice Department and restore public confidence after the controversies of Gonzales’s tenure.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-Calif., also opposed Mukasey, citing his unwillingness to declare waterboarding illegal. Feinstein said the issue was not theoretical and that the nation needed an attorney general willing to draw clear limits on interrogation practices.

The vote reflected divisions within both parties, though most Republicans backed Mukasey and most Democrats opposed him. His confirmation gave President George W. Bush a new attorney general at a time when the administration faced continuing scrutiny over national security programs, executive power and the treatment of detainees in the war on terrorism.

Mukasey initially drew bipartisan praise because he was viewed as independent and legally serious. But his confirmation became a major fight in the Senate Judiciary Committee over one issue in particular: waterboarding. He called the practice “repugnant” and said torture was unconstitutional, but he argued that he did not know enough about the classified details of CIA interrogation methods to give a definitive legal judgment. The Judiciary Committee fight was especially tense because Democrats controlled the panel. Chairman Patrick Leahy and most committee Democrats opposed Mukasey after his waterboarding answers. However, two Democrats—Charles Schumer, who had originally recommended Mukasey, and Dianne Feinstein—joined Republicans in voting to send the nomination to the full Senate. The committee approved him 11–8.

The full Senate confirmed Mukasey on November 8, 2007, by a narrow 53–40 vote, making him one of the more controversial attorney general confirmations in modern times. The vote reflected both frustration with the Bush administration’s post-9/11 legal policies and reluctance by some senators to leave the Justice Department leaderless after the Gonzales resignation.

Public opinion on torture at the time was mixed rather than overwhelmingly opposed. Polls in the mid-2000s generally showed Americans divided: many said torture could be justified at least sometimes to obtain information from suspected terrorists, while a substantial minority or near-half said it was rarely or never justified. That ambivalence helped shape the politics of the Mukasey fight: civil-liberties groups and many Democrats treated waterboarding as a bright-line legal and moral issue, while the White House and many Republicans argued for flexibility in counterterrorism interrogations and resisted labeling specific CIA methods illegal.

(CNN) -- Michael Mukasey, a retired federal judge and former prosecutor, took over as attorney general at a moment when the Justice Department was struggling to restore its credibility after months of political turmoil under Alberto Gonzales — and as the Bush administration faced renewed scrutiny over the limits of presidential power in the war on terror.

Mukasey’s arrival followed Gonzales’ resignation amid bipartisan criticism over the firing of U.S. attorneys, questions about political influence inside the Justice Department and disputes over the administration’s domestic surveillance and interrogation policies.

President George W. Bush cast Mukasey as a steady hand who could rebuild confidence in the department. Supporters pointed to his long tenure on the federal bench, including his handling of terrorism-related cases in New York, and argued that he brought independence and legal seriousness to a department battered by controversy.

But Mukasey’s confirmation process quickly became entangled in the same national security debates that had dogged his predecessor.

At the center of the dispute was whether certain harsh interrogation techniques — particularly waterboarding — amounted to torture under U.S. law. Mukasey declined during Senate hearings to declare the practice illegal in all circumstances, saying he had not been fully briefed on classified interrogation programs and did not want to make a legal judgment without knowing the facts.

That answer angered many Democrats and human rights advocates, who said the nation’s top law enforcement officer should be able to state plainly that waterboarding is torture. Several senators argued that the refusal reflected a broader unwillingness by the administration to repudiate post-September 11 policies that expanded executive authority.

Republicans and some moderate Democrats countered that Mukasey was being cautious rather than evasive. They said his experience and temperament made him the best candidate available to stabilize the Justice Department, even if his answers on interrogation left critics unsatisfied.

The debate underscored the difficult terrain Mukasey inherited. The Justice Department was not only dealing with the fallout from the U.S. attorney firings but also defending controversial surveillance programs authorized after the 2001 terrorist attacks. Those programs raised persistent questions about warrantless monitoring, the role of the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court and whether telecommunications companies should receive legal immunity for assisting the government.

Civil liberties groups warned that Mukasey’s confirmation could signal continuity with the administration’s expansive view of presidential power. White House officials, meanwhile, insisted that aggressive intelligence tools were necessary to prevent attacks and that the programs operated within the law.

For Mukasey, the challenge was immediate: reassure Congress and the public that the Justice Department would enforce the law independently while also serving an administration determined to preserve its counterterrorism authorities.

His tenure began with expectations that he would bring calm to an agency shaken by scandal. But the fights over interrogation, surveillance and executive power made clear that the controversies of the Gonzales era would not disappear with a change in leadership.

**Senate Approves Mukasey Nomination After Democratic Split Over Waterboarding**

WASHINGTON — The Senate approved Michael B. Mukasey’s nomination to become attorney general, ending a contentious confirmation fight dominated less by his legal résumé than by his refusal to declare waterboarding illegal.

Mukasey, a retired federal judge from New York, was nominated by President George W. Bush to replace Alberto Gonzales, whose tenure at the Justice Department was marked by controversy over warrantless surveillance, interrogation policy and the firing of U.S. attorneys. Mukasey’s supporters portrayed him as an independent-minded jurist who could restore credibility to the department. But his confirmation became a test of how far senators were willing to go in demanding a clear repudiation of harsh interrogation tactics used in the fight against terrorism.

The Senate confirmed Mukasey despite significant Democratic opposition. The vote reflected a deep split among Democrats, some of whom argued that the Justice Department urgently needed new leadership and that Mukasey was preferable to leaving the department under acting leadership. Others said his unwillingness to call waterboarding torture made him unacceptable for the nation’s top law-enforcement post.

### Why Democrats Were Divided

Democratic senators who supported Mukasey, including some who had praised his judicial record and independence, said they were troubled by his answers on interrogation but believed he was qualified and would be an improvement over the outgoing Justice Department leadership. They also argued that blocking the nomination might prolong instability at the department and could leave in place officials more closely tied to the Bush administration’s disputed legal policies.

Opponents countered that the issue was not merely semantic. They said the attorney general must be able to state plainly that waterboarding — an interrogation method that simulates drowning — is torture and therefore illegal. For them, Mukasey’s refusal raised doubts about whether he would enforce anti-torture statutes, review past legal opinions authorizing harsh interrogation, or resist White House pressure on national security matters.

The Democratic divide was especially striking because criticism of the Bush administration’s interrogation program had become a central issue for many in the party. Some senators viewed Mukasey as a conservative but credible nominee; others saw his position on waterboarding as disqualifying.

### What Mukasey Said About Waterboarding

During his confirmation hearings and in written responses to senators, Mukasey repeatedly refused to give a definitive legal judgment on whether waterboarding is torture.

He said he found waterboarding personally “repugnant” and suggested that if the technique were performed as commonly described, it would seem to be “over the line” and “hypothetical” conduct that could violate the law. But he stopped short of declaring it illegal.

Mukasey gave several reasons for that refusal. He said he had not been briefed on the exact methods used by U.S. intelligence agencies and did not want to issue a legal opinion without knowing the facts. He also said that publicly labeling a specific interrogation method illegal could expose U.S. personnel to legal jeopardy or signal limits to adversaries.

His critics said those explanations were inadequate because waterboarding has long been recognized by U.S. authorities and human rights groups as torture. They argued that a nominee for attorney general did not need access to classified details to answer whether simulated drowning is prohibited under U.S. and international law.

### Poll Shows Public Skepticism of Waterboarding

The debate unfolded as a CNN/Opinion Research Corporation poll showed broad public concern about the practice.

According to the poll, **69 percent of Americans said they considered waterboarding to be torture**, while **29 percent said they did not**. The survey also found that **58 percent said the U.S. government should not be allowed to use waterboarding on suspected terrorists**, while **40 percent said it should be allowed**.

Those results underscored the political difficulty surrounding Mukasey’s nomination. While the Bush administration avoided publicly confirming details of interrogation methods used by the CIA, many Americans viewed waterboarding as torture and opposed its use.

### A Confirmation With Lingering Questions

Mukasey’s approval gave the Justice Department a new leader at a critical moment, but it did not settle the broader dispute over interrogation policy. Instead, his confirmation highlighted the continuing tension between national security claims and legal limits on executive power.

For supporters, Mukasey represented a chance to stabilize and repair a Justice Department battered by scandal. For opponents, his refusal to clearly condemn waterboarding suggested that the department might continue to avoid accountability for some of the most controversial policies of the post-September 11 era.
